question: What is area navigation (RNAV)?

options.text: Navigation only along airways joining ground beacons
Navigation by dead reckoning without any inputs
Flying any desired track within coverage
Navigation using a single VOR at a time

explanation: RNAV allows the aircraft to fly any desired track within the coverage of station-referenced signals, or within the limits of a self-contained system, without flying over the ground aids.

question: Which RNAV input is self-contained, needing no outside signal?
explanation: RNAV can use VOR/DME, ILS/MLS, GNSS, INS/IRS, air data and time. Only the inertial system works entirely on its own, which is why it is blended with external references whose accuracy does not decay.

question: Which is a benefit of RNAV routes?

options.text: Aircraft can fly without any ATC clearance
Shorter routes, saving time and fuel
Aircraft no longer need a flight plan
Vertical separation is no longer needed

explanation: More direct routes save distance, time and fuel; parallel and bypass routes increase capacity; and separation criteria can be reduced.

question: What accuracy must Basic RNAV (B-RNAV) achieve?

options.text: ±1 NM on at least 95% of occasions
±0.3 NM on at least 95% of occasions
±5 NM on at least 95% of occasions

explanation: B-RNAV requires 5 NM accuracy 95% of the time; P-RNAV requires 1 NM.

question: What accuracy must Precision RNAV (P-RNAV) achieve?

options.text: ±5 NM on at least 95% of occasions
±2 NM on at least 95% of occasions
±1 NM on at least 95% of occasions

explanation: P-RNAV requires 1 NM accuracy 95% of the time and is used in terminal airspace.

question: Where are P-RNAV routes being established?
explanation: P-RNAV, with its tighter accuracy, is used for terminal routes such as SIDs and STARs.

question: What does 3D RNAV add to 2D RNAV?
explanation: 2D works in the horizontal plane only; 3D adds vertical guidance; 4D adds a timing function to 3D.

question: What does 4D RNAV add to 3D RNAV?
explanation: 4D RNAV adds time (for example, required time of arrival) to lateral and vertical navigation.

question: Which components make up a simple 2D RNAV system on the flight deck?

options.text: Nav computer, CDU, CDI or HSI

explanation: A simple system has a navigation computer unit, a control and display unit, and a course deviation indicator or HSI.

question: How does a simple 2D RNAV system define its waypoints?

options.text: As a range and bearing from a VOR/DME
As a time and heading from the departure point
As a QDM from an NDB
As latitude and longitude from GNSS

explanation: Each waypoint is entered as a radial and distance from a suitably placed VOR/DME. The system then treats it as if it were a beacon.

question: Why are 2D RNAV waypoints sometimes called "phantom stations"?

options.text: They are stations that have been withdrawn
They exist only in the database, not on charts
They can be received only at night
Each waypoint is shown as if it were a VOR/DME

explanation: The computer gives course and distance to the waypoint as though a VOR/DME were there, so it is a "phantom" beacon.

question: How is cross-track deviation shown on a simple 2D RNAV system?
explanation: Unlike a VOR, which shows angular deviation, RNAV shows linear deviation from the computed track in NM.

question: What happens when an ILS frequency is entered as an RNAV waypoint?

options.text: The RNAV computes a phantom ILS
The ILS is ignored by the RNAV
The RNAV shows the ILS DME only
The instruments revert to ILS mode

explanation: Selecting an ILS frequency as a waypoint switches the instrumentation automatically to ILS mode.

question: A 2D RNAV is about to fly from WP1 to WP2, defined from beacon POL. What does it need to compute the track and distance?

options.text: Its own and WP2's positions relative to POL
The distance between the two VORs only
The aircraft's heading and true airspeed
The bearing of WP2 from the aircraft's NDB

explanation: Knowing two sides of the triangle (aircraft to POL, POL to WP2) and the included angle referenced to magnetic north, it solves for track and distance, then computes cross-track error continuously.

question: What must the pilot check about each waypoint of a simple RNAV route?

options.text: It is within 25 NM of an NDB
It is on a published airway
It is within the DOC of the VOR/DMEs used
It is defined by two different VORs

explanation: Each waypoint must be within the designated operational coverage of the VOR/DME defining it and of the one defining the next waypoint.

question: Why must data be entered carefully into a simple RNAV CDU?

options.text: The CDU deletes data after one hour
The computer cannot recognise input errors
Each entry can be made only once per flight
The computer rejects any waypoint beyond 25 NM

explanation: The computer will fly whatever is entered; it cannot detect or correct a wrong radial or distance.

question: When is the along-track accuracy of a 2D RNAV fix best?

options.text: When the VOR/DME is close to the track line
When the VOR/DME is outside its DOC
When the aircraft is directly over the VOR/DME
When the VOR/DME is at right angles to the track

explanation: If the station lies near the track, the DME range runs along the track and gives good along-track accuracy. A station abeam the track gives the best across-track accuracy.

question: What DME error must be considered when choosing facilities close to track?
explanation: Close to and high above a DME, slant range differs significantly from ground range, which affects the computed position.

question: In a modern airliner, which unit performs the area navigation function?
explanation: The FMC provides navigation, guidance and performance functions, using inputs from IRS, radio aids, air data and fuel systems.

question: Which is a requirement of a 4D RNAV system?

options.text: Display cross-track error only on the PFD
Execute a modified flight plan only after crew action
Change the flight plan automatically without crew input
Use the local datum of each country

explanation: Requirements include crew confirmation before executing changes, automatic waypoint sequencing with turn anticipation, direct-to, parallel offsets, holds, estimates of position uncertainty, WGS-84 and failure indication.

question: Which geodetic reference system must a 4D RNAV system conform to?
explanation: RNAV systems must use the WGS-84 global datum, so that database positions and GNSS positions agree.

question: Which items make up the B737-800 flight management system?

options.text: FMCS, weather radar, TCAS and GPWS
FMCS, VOR, DME and ADF only

explanation: The FMS joins the flight management computer system, the AFDS, the autothrottle and two IRSs into one integrated system.

question: Which four dimensions does the FMS navigate in?
explanation: The FMS provides 4D area navigation and optimises performance for the most economical flight.

question: Which is a function that only the crew can carry out, even with full FMS operation?
explanation: Thrust initiation, take-off, altitude selection, ILS tuning, configuration and landing rollout are crew actions. The crew must monitor the FMC throughout.

question: How does the FMC combine IRS and radio position inputs?
explanation: Kalman filtering blends the short-term accuracy of the IRS with the long-term accuracy of the external reference to produce a best estimate of position and velocity.

question: What does the crew see if the FMS is using IRS information alone for position?

options.text: An automatic disconnection of the autopilot
A warning that position accuracy is downgraded
A request to enter a new position
No indication; the IRS is always accurate

explanation: Without radio updating the position is flagged as downgraded.

question: What does the FMC performance database contain?

options.text: Performance data and the cost index strategy

explanation: The performance database holds the aircraft's performance parameters and the company's cost index strategy. The navigation database holds aerodromes, navaids, airways, procedures and company routes.

question: Which item is held in the FMC navigation database?
explanation: The navigation database contains aerodromes and runways, navaids (position, altitude, frequency, ident, DOC), airways and reporting points, SIDs, STARs, approaches and company routes.

question: How often is the FMC navigation database updated?
explanation: Updates follow the international 28-day (AIRAC) cycle, and the FMC holds the current and next periods.

question: What are the line select keys (LSKs) on a CDU used for?

options.text: Inserting or selecting data, changing pages
Tuning the VOR and ILS manually

explanation: LSKs beside the screen insert data from the scratchpad into a field, select data down to the scratchpad, and move through pages.

question: Where on the CDU is data typed before it is inserted?

options.text: The title line at the top of the screen
The scratchpad at the bottom of the screen

explanation: Data is typed into the scratchpad, then inserted into the correct field with an LSK.

question: On a CDU, what do boxed fields indicate?

options.text: Data that is out of date

explanation: Boxes show essential data (e.g. the IRS position); dashes show optional data (e.g. heading to speed alignment).

question: On the IDENT page, which item can the crew change?
explanation: Only the active nav data can be changed: select the next period down to the scratchpad and insert it into the active line.

question: On the POS INIT page, why might the crew enter the magnetic heading?

options.text: To speed up IRS alignment after a move
To select the departure runway and the SID to be flown

explanation: Entering the heading from the standby compass helps alignment, particularly if the aircraft has been moved.

question: After activating a route on the CDU, what must the crew do?

options.text: Press the NEXT PAGE key twice

explanation: Selecting ACTIVATE lights the EXEC key, which must be pressed for the computer to use the route.

question: Which latitude/longitude entry would a CDU accept?
explanation: Positions use a 7-character (e.g. N05W010) or 15-character format, and leading zeros must be included.

question: Up to how many characters may an aerodrome, navaid or airway designator have in the FMC?
explanation: Up to 5 alphanumerics for aerodromes, reporting points, navaids, airways and runways; up to 7 for SIDs and STARs.

question: A pilot enters TRN250/76. What will the FMC create?

options.text: A point 250°/76 NM from TRN, named TRN01
A waypoint 250 NM from TRN on bearing 076°
A course of 250° to intercept TRN at 76 NM
A hold at TRN with a 76-second leg

explanation: This is a place-bearing/distance (PBD) waypoint. The FMC names it TRN01 if it is the first defined from TRN.

question: What does an entry such as GOW167.0/TRN090.5 create?

options.text: A route from GOW to TRN at FL 167
A waypoint where the two bearings intersect
A hold at GOW with a 90.5 s leg

explanation: Bearing/bearing (course intersection) waypoints are where a bearing from one database point crosses a bearing from another. Bearings must be 3 or 5 digits.

question: Unless changed, what speed restriction does the CLB page apply?

options.text: 250 kt below FL 100 only on SIDs

explanation: The climb speed restriction defaults to 250/10 000. ATC restrictions can be entered from the scratchpad.

question: On an FMC page, what does the suffix "A" after an altitude mean?
explanation: 6000A means at or above 6 000 ft.

question: What does the CRZ page show at its centre top line?
explanation: The cruise page shows current cruise altitude, target speed, N1, predicted destination fuel, optimum and maximum levels, step climb details and wind.

question: On the descent page, what default speed transition is used if none is defined?
explanation: The descent speed transition is 10 kt less than the database value, defaulting to 240/10 000.

question: On the descent page, what is V/B?

options.text: The path angle needed for the next constraint

explanation: V/B (vertical bearing) is the path angle required to meet the next constraint. FPA is the actual angle and V/S the actual rate of descent.

question: With twin IRS, why does the FMC need an external reference?

options.text: The IRS works only in the air after the alignment is complete
The IRS provides no ground speed
It cannot tell which IRS is wrong

explanation: Two IRSs that disagree give no way of telling which is in error. An external reference (DME/DME, VOR/DME or GNSS) resolves it.

question: How does Kalman filtering weight IRS and external inputs as a flight goes on?

options.text: External reference favoured at first; then the IRS
IRS favoured at first; then the external reference

explanation: The IRS is most accurate early on, but its errors grow with time, so the weighting gradually shifts towards the external reference.

question: In the dual mode of a twin FMS, why may the EFIS position differ from each CDU position?

options.text: Each CDU shows the IRS position only
The EFIS shows the position one minute ahead
The EFIS uses only GNSS position

explanation: Each FMC finds its own position; these are compared for gross errors before the result is passed to the EFIS.

question: With both FMCs failed, what is still available?

options.text: IRS information displayed directly on the EFIS

explanation: The IRS can feed the EFIS directly, but automatic performance functions are lost.

question: With triple IRS, what does the FMC do with the three positions?

options.text: Checks for gross errors, then averages

explanation: The three are compared to reject any with a gross error, averaged, and then blended with external references by Kalman filtering.

question: Above what latitude does the FMC decouple from a blended IRS position?
explanation: Above 84°, each FMC uses a single IRS (left in the order left, centre, right; right in the order right, centre, left).

question: Why does the FMC decouple the IRS positions at very high latitude?

options.text: The IRS cannot sense the earth's rotation there
Small errors give large changes of longitude there
The magnetic compass becomes unreliable there
GNSS satellites are not visible there

explanation: Change of longitude depends on the secant of latitude, which grows very rapidly near 90°. Tiny latitude errors cause large apparent longitude divergence between IRSs.

question: How does IRS position accuracy typically change during a flight?

options.text: It degrades by roughly 1 NM per hour
It degrades by roughly 10 NM per hour
It improves as the flight goes on

explanation: IRS position error grows steadily (about 1 NM/h), although heading and ground speed stay accurate.

question: What is the maximum DME error at 100 NM?
After several hours of flight, which gives the more accurate position: DME/DME fixing or IRS?

options.text: IRS, because DME has slant range error
DME/DME: its error does not grow

explanation: DME error is constant for a given range; IRS error grows with time. After several hours DME fixing is much better.

question: When is the FMC position most accurate during a flight?

options.text: After the runway update, and on ILS/MLS final
At the top of climb, once the IRS has settled

explanation: The position is best just after the runway update, decays towards the accuracy of the external reference, and improves again on final approach with ILS or MLS.
